newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Reform awaits election bill.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CONGRESS WEEK-Reform awaits election bill.

text.p: Rivalries between the government's political allies were expected to dominate this week in Congress when a bill outlining the rules for next year's elections was due to reach the floor of the Chamber of Deputies.

With political party bosses haggling over the contents of the bill, there was no chance of a second, full vote on the government's civil service reform bill until next week at the earliest, a spokeswoman for the government in Congress said.

"The election bill is always polemical because it strikes right at the heart of lawmakers' interests," the spokeswoman said. "The vote might not happen until next week and civil service reform will just have to wait."
Brazil faces presidential, state governorship and congressional elections in October 1998. A law setting rules for campaigning has to be through both houses of Congress by October this year.

Despite the looming deadline, however, the government and its allies are at loggerheads over several items in a rough draft of the bill, including proposed restrictions on campaign funding and television airtime.

The government also wants to do away with an article that would prevent President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and governors seeking re-election from inaugurating public works, traditionally a big vote-winning tactic in Brazil.

Other business on the schedule in the Chamber of Deputies this week included a bill which would extend financing opportunities for the construction sector and an inquiry into alleged misuse of parliamentary perks by lawmakers.
In the Senate, the government's pension reform bill was set to return to a committee after receiving more than 30 proposed amendments in initial discussions on the upper house floor.

An aide to Sen. Beni Veras, who is in charge of the bill in the Senate, said a first of two full votes on the reform might yet take place next week, but said the end of the month was a more realistic target.

The pension reform bill, once approved in the Senate, will have to go back to the Chamber of Deputies for approval of changes made in the upper house. Many political analysts have questioned whether it will make it through Congress before next year's elections.
